desc:
In the m x n matrix grid, every row is sorted in non-decreasing order from left to right, and every column is sorted in non-decreasing order from top to bottom. Values may repeat.

Return the k-th smallest value when all m * n cells are put in sorted order (so duplicates count separately: in [1, 1, 2] the 2nd smallest is 1). Try to avoid sorting all the cells.
constraints: Each row and each column is in non-decreasing order
hints: Flattening and sorting works in O(mn log(mn)). The row and column order should let you do better.
Instead of searching positions, search values: for a number x, how many cells are ≤ x? Can you count that without looking at every cell?

Count cells ≤ x by walking a staircase from the bottom-left corner: move up when the cell is greater than x, otherwise count the column prefix and move right. Binary search the smallest x in [grid[0][0], grid[m-1][n-1]] whose count is at least k.
editorial: The answer is a value that exists in the grid, lying between the top-left and bottom-right cells. Define count(x) as the number of cells with value ≤ x; it never decreases as x grows. The k-th smallest value is the smallest x with count(x) ≥ k, and that x is always an actual cell value, because count only jumps at values present in the grid.

Compute count(x) in O(m + n): begin at the bottom-left cell; if it exceeds x move up, otherwise all cells above it in this column are ≤ x, so add row + 1 and move right. Binary search over the value range takes about 31 iterations, for O((m + n) log(range)) time and O(1) space. A min-heap that pops k times is another option at O(k log m).
